claim: Enough does not modify the core degree determinatives: enough money (or money enough), not ∗much enough money.
evidence_summary: OED quotations with sufficiency enough after few: For a relatively short accelerator, there may be few enough grids so that a considerable fraction of the ion beam penetrates all the grids (J. C. Slater, Microwave Electronics, 1950, under grid, n.¹); A number of persons who communicate with one another often over a span of time, and..few enough so that each person is able to communicate with all the others..face-to-face (G. C. Homans, Human Group, 1950, under primary group, n.). Every little enough found in determiner function has the understatement sense “very little”: There was little enough comfort for us subalterns (A. Griffiths, 1904); Little enough encouragement was there (Lancet, 1946); have little enough money left for reinvestment except in technology (C. Coker, Humane Warfare, 2001). Few enough men and scarcely any women can tell the difference (Illustrated American, 1893) is the same use. OED quotation searches find no many enough, and one much enough, a 1562 proverb about the word itself: This woord enough twoo waies we may skan. Thone much enough, thother littell enough (J. Heywood).
finding: Sufficiency enough modifies few, in determiner function in Slater and also in Homans, where a group is defined by its size; the restriction fails for few. A defender could read Slater as understatement followed by a separate result clause, but that reading doesn’t fit Homans’s definition. The evidence is two quotations, both from 1950. CGEL doesn’t define “core”, but §7.11 and §11(c) (p. 431) both name many, much, few and little. No sufficiency little enough in determiner function was found: those quotations are the understatement use. The OED (enough, revised 2020) separates an intensive adverb sense (“fully, quite, pretty, very”) from “Sufficiently” but doesn’t place little enough in either, so treating it as the intensive use is an inference. For much and many the OED quotations agree with CGEL: many enough has no hits, and the one much enough is a 1562 proverb about the word enough.
proposed_wording: Note, however, that in this sense it doesn’t modify much, many or little: we have enough money (or money enough), not ∗much enough money. It can modify few: there may be few enough grids so that a considerable fraction of the ion beam penetrates all the grids. Little enough in determiner function has the understatement sense “very little” (There was little enough comfort for us subalterns).
inference: Does sufficiency enough combine with any core degree determinative?

evidence.source: Oxford English Dictionary, quotation search for “few enough”.
evidence.example: 1950 For a relatively short accelerator, there may be few enough grids so that a considerable fraction of the ion beam penetrates all the grids (J. C. Slater, Microwave Electronics, under grid, n.¹). 1950 A number of persons who communicate with one another often over a span of time, and..few enough so that each person is able to communicate with all the others..face-to-face (G. C. Homans, Human Group, under primary group, n.). 1893 Few enough men and scarcely any women can tell the difference… (Illustr. Amer., under built, adj.) has the understatement sense.
evidence.establishes: Sufficiency enough with few in edited prose, in determiner function before a plural head in Slater. The so that clause fixes the sufficiency reading; Homans’s definition of a group by its size can’t be read as understatement.
evidence.locator: Quotation search, 5 results. Accessed 19 November 2026 through the University of Toronto Libraries subscription.

evidence.source: Oxford English Dictionary, quotation search for “little enough”.
evidence.example: 1904 There was little enough comfort for us subalterns (A. Griffiths, under planking, n.). 1944 we have had little enough success in charming the ear of the nation (Theology, under nation, n.¹). 1946 Little enough encouragement was there… (Lancet, under poitrinaire, n.). 2001 have little enough money left for reinvestment except in technology (C. Coker, Humane Warfare, under reinvestment, n.).
evidence.establishes: Little enough in determiner function, with the understatement sense “very little” in every case found, not sufficiency. These count against CGEL only if that use is the same enough.
evidence.locator: Quotation search, 32 results. Accessed 19 November 2026 through the University of Toronto Libraries subscription.

evidence.example: Adverb sense 2: “Fully; quite; used after adjectives to express slight augmentation of the positive degree, and sometimes equivalent to very”, listed apart from adverb sense 1, “Sufficiently”. Determiner sense 1 (“Sufficient”) has the constructed example We had little enough time to finish the project.
evidence.establishes: Some support for treating understatement little enough as a separate use, though Wiktionary also files a little enough example under sufficiency.
evidence.locator: English, Determiner sense 1 and Adverb sense 2. Accessed 19 November 2026.

evidence.source: Oxford English Dictionary, “enough, adj., pron., n., adv.” (revised 2020).
evidence.example: Adverb sense 1a: “Sufficiently; in a quantity or degree that satisfies a desire, meets a want, or fulfils a purpose”. Sense 2: “With the idea of satisfying a requirement reduced or absent”; 2a “With intensive force: fully, quite, pretty, very, as much as well could be”; 2a(i) “Modifying an adjective or adverb. Now esp. in certain set phrases” (fair enough, like enough, right enough, sure enough, well enough).
evidence.establishes: The OED separates an intensive enough from sufficiency enough, which gives the understatement reading of little enough a recognized source. The entry doesn’t classify little enough itself, and no OED entry or definition contains it.
evidence.locator: Meaning & use, part C (adverb), senses 1a, 2, 2a, 2a(i). The entry text, including collapsed quotations, has no little, few, much or many enough. Accessed 19 November 2026 through the University of Toronto Libraries subscription.

evidence.source: Oxford English Dictionary, quotation search for “much enough”.
evidence.example: 1562 This woord enough twoo waies we may skan. Thone much enough, thother littell enough (J. Heywood, Prov., under scan, v.).
evidence.establishes: No much enough with the sufficiency sense or in determiner function. The one hit is about the word enough itself.
evidence.locator: Quotation search, 1 result. Accessed 19 November 2026 through the University of Toronto Libraries subscription.

evidence.source: Oxford English Dictionary, quotation search for “many enough”.
evidence.establishes: No many enough in the OED quotations. An absence from a quotation corpus is consistent with CGEL’s restriction but doesn’t prove it.
